item.title: My Software development principles
item.description:
This is a test to put into words what I have learned and believe about software development. Will probably change when learn more so this blog post will probably be updated. There are two parts, principles, ideas I consider proven, and hypotheses, ideas that seem reasonable but that I want to test more before considering them proven.

Of course these ideas are context specific and should be tested and evaluated in your own context. My thinking is mostly in the context of supporting company internal users with an engineering environment.

item.title: What is an engineering strategy
item.description:
If you are some kind of leader in software development you have probably followed and/or been expected to produce an engineering strategy. I have written strategies, I have read many strategies but I come back to the question about what an engineering strategy really is. And the best definition I have found is Will Larson’s Writing an engineering strategy

He uses Richard Rumelt’s framework.

  • Diagnosis: a theory describing the nature of the challenge.
  • Guiding policies: the approaches you’ll apply to grapple with the challenge.
  • Coherent actions: a set of specific actions directed by guiding policy to address challenge.

Go read the article to get all you need, examples, how and when to write it, how to relate to other company strategies and more.

item.title: The Consulting Detective´s Guide to Software Development: Lessons from Sherlock Holmes
item.description:
As an avid Sherlock Holmes reader and software engineer, I asked myself if the methods of the greatest detective are useful in a software development context. This isn’t a handbook on software development, but wouldn’t your day be a little more exciting if you approached it like Sherlock Holmes? Here are key lessons developers can learn from the master of deduction:

Partner for Perspective

"I am lost without my Boswell." — A Scandal in Bohemia

Holmes relied on Watson not just for companionship, but for his different perspective and complementary skills. In software development, collaboration brings diverse viewpoints that catch blind spots and spark innovation. No developer possesses every skill or perspective needed to build exceptional software. Find your Watson—someone whose strengths balance your weaknesses—and you’ll solve problems more effectively together.

item.title: Events in CICD
item.description:
What do you do when you have a large scale setup of build, integration, test and release pipelines that continuously evolve?

At Ericsson, we have used events in CI/CD for many years (Ericsson blog post). This approach gives us valuable flexibility — we can quickly adapt CI/CD pipelines to meet new product requirements. Whether it’s setting up a new integration pipeline for a product variant, reusing test results from another pipeline, or triggering pipelines based on upstream results, event-driven architectures make it (relatively) easy.

item.title: What’s Slowing You Down? Diving into Lead Time for Changes
item.description:
When assessing how to measure the effectiveness of a development organization, one useful metric is “how quickly can we make a change?” This idea is not new—DORA metrics, for example, include “Lead Time for Changes.”

While we didn’t go into detailed definitions, we considered lead time as the duration from identifying a need to having a solution deployed and in use. I wanted to explore what factors influence this measurement and what we should focus on if we want to improve it.

item.title: Book review: Ask your developer
item.description: Ask Your Developer: How to Harness the Power of Software Developers and Win in the 21st Century by Jeff Lawson was the book that influenced me the most last year. It is about how to run a software development company and the main theme is what the title says, use your developers competence and problems solving competence. Give them problems that you want them to solve instead of detailed descriptions of what to do. item.title: Why I write 2
item.description:
When I started this blog I said that I want to do it mostly for myself. Andy Hawthorne says something similar, Why Blog If Nobody Reads It?.

“Like blogging. You write because you think, because you observe, because you need to put it somewhere. If someone reads it? Bonus. If not? The work still got done.”

And after reading Build a link blog I want to add that I could use the blog as a way to remember good links and what I was thinking when reading them.

item.title: Chesterton´s fence and being proud of what you have
item.description:
Chesterton’s fence is “the principle that reforms should not be made until the reasoning behind the existing state of affairs is understood.” Wikipedia. In software development think about is as don’t change code or an architecture before you understand why it is the way it is.

This is a good principle but I also started thinking about it from another perspective. When looking at an existing solution we as software engineers and developers can be very critical, this is not good, we have better ways to solve these kind of problems, let’s migrate, use a new technology. Yes we could probably improve the solution, the industry changes fast. But don’t forget to be proud! The solution is there, adds value, sometimes it has been doing that for a long time. Give it a chance and remember that when it was designed the decision were based on other requirements and possibilities than you have today. And this can help your reason. Do you really need to change it? Are the requirements that different now? Is this a dinosaur or could it be a technological shark that still is a good way to solve the problem?

item.title: Book review: Modern software engineering
item.description: Modern software engineering written by David Farley is a good book to read if you want an overview of a systematic approach to software development that has focus on real delivering real impact instead of where we many times end up planning and focusing on being busy. It is not about throwing away process. It is about a systematic approach (this is engineering) and making use of what makes software different from many other areas, we can create, run, learn from and change the software in minutes. A short summary would be - waterfall is not a good practice in software development, make use of the superpower of short experiments. The book adds on a lot to this, measure, test, characteristics of good software and also some perspectives on the people and organisation that works with the software.

item.title: Book review: The unicorn project
item.description: The Unicorn project is a book about how to (and how not to) develop software in a large company. How do you go from an inefficient, slow and frustrating work environment to a setup where you deliver value fast and people are happy to go to work? Gene Kim’s (the author) answer is DevOps, create teams that understand the business, can work end to end from business need to deployed software and that can do experiments, learn from the deployment and improve.

item.title: Internal development platform principles
item.description:
Reflections on internal development platform (IDP) development.

Solve user problems, don’t build perfect tools

There is a risk in focusing too much on building the “perfect” tool while neglecting deployment and user experience. As an internal team, you have the unique advantage of direct access to your users. Leverage this proximity: collaborate closely with them, understand their needs, create solutions, deploy quickly, gather feedback, and iterate. Your mission is to deliver a great user experience that aligns with and supports the company’s mission.

item.title: What is (software) architecture
item.description:
What is software architecture? And is it needed?

I met Charity Majors at a conference recently and talked to her about her statement “architect is a bullshit role”. I am one of those that she refers to when she says “One of my favorite things in the world is when software architects come up to me and tell me how much they enjoyed my piece about how “software architect” is such a bullshit role at most companies.”

item.title: Death to the program! Long live the project.
item.description:
Maybe a niche thing to reflect on, but some software companies went from projects to programs. Why start projects all the time, let’s just define a never ending project and call it program. In many cases I don’t think it works very well.

  • Programs get the wrong focus. A project exist to deliver a value before a deadline. A program does not have specific deliverables or deadlines. They can have it for activities that are part of the program but the program leadership do not own the responsibility for delivering on time and they tend to instead focus on being busy. Focus tends to go from flow optimization to resource optimization.
  • Programs never end which means that you don’t get natural points when you hopefully celebrate achievements. You also don’t get the natural times to reflect, recover and clean up. You are always busy (see the point above.)

Programs can probably be a good tool when you have a predictable process that you want to run over and over again, usually with similar outputs. This is however not what software developent looks like.

item.title: Does is matter if I call it a PoC or MVP?
item.description: In software development we run Proof of Concepts (PoCs), do Minimum Viable Products (MVPs), use DevOps and many other activities that have names that are more or less well defined. So when I want to get something done, does it matter what I call it? Yes! Or a longer answer, Yes, it matters in the context where other people interact with your activity, people that finance it, use the output or might fight against it.

item.title: How long is a Poc?
item.description: In software development many do proof of concepts (PoC), “a realization of a certain idea, method or principle in order to demonstrate its feasibility, or viability, or a demonstration in principle with the aim of verifying that some concept or theory has practical potential.” In this post I wanted to get an understanding of if there is some kind of de facto agreement on the lenght of PoCs. (Part of trying to answer the question How fast is fast in software development?) Why? In many organisations I have seen the term PoC being used for long projects (months, years) and I think there is a value in having a common understanding in terms that we use, such as PoCs. Otherwise you might have very different expectations on the activity.

item.title: Death to the software pipeline!
item.description:
CI pipelines, CD pipelines, devops pipelines, why do we talk so much about pipelines?

A recent discussion on LinkedIn, along with an example from my own work, made me realize something: we need to stop obsessing over the “pipelines” themselves! The issue is that when we focus on the pipeline we forget about why we have them, to automate the value adding activities we want to run before deploying or shipping. If teams focus more on pipeline engine selection and logic than what you actually want to do in the pipeline you focus on the wrong things.

item.title: How not to get stuck with solutions to problems you helped fix
item.description: As a senior developer or technical leader, you are often called in to solve urgent problems. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that—it’s often part of your job description. However, after fixing the immediate issue, there’s a risk that you get drawn into a continuous cycle of improving that area. You’ve resolved a critical problem and are now seen as a key person for that domain, and this pattern repeats as you get pulled into other firefighting activities.

item.title: My motivation for blogging
item.description:
Why do I write this blog?

To help myself think. Improve my reasoning. Test ideas.

To improve my writing. Writing is an important way of communication as a technical leader.

And maybe it is useful for someone else.
